# How Cells Make and Use Energy

## The cell theory

The cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the processes of life. Every living organism is made of one or more cells, and every cell comes from a cell that existed before it. These three ideas together are called the cell theory. Before microscopes improved in the seventeenth century, nobody could see cells at all, so the theory had to wait for better lenses. Today the cell theory is the starting point for the rest of biology, because every process described later in these notes happens inside or between cells. Single-celled organisms such as bacteria carry out every life process in one cell, while a human body contains tens of trillions of cells that divide the work between them. Even so, each of those cells still follows the same basic rules about energy, information and membranes.

## Membranes control what enters and leaves

Every cell is surrounded by a plasma membrane that controls what enters and leaves the cell. The membrane is built from a phospholipid bilayer: two layers of molecules whose water-loving heads face outward and whose water-fearing tails face each other in the middle. Small uncharged molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide slip straight through the bilayer by diffusion, moving from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated. Charged ions and large molecules such as glucose cannot cross on their own and need help from proteins embedded in the membrane. Some of these proteins form channels that let particular substances through, while pumps use energy to move substances against their concentration gradient. Because the membrane is selective, a cell can keep its inside chemistry very different from its surroundings.

## Mitochondria and cellular respiration

Mitochondria produce most of the cell's usable energy in the form of ATP through cellular respiration. Cellular respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water as waste products. The process begins in the cytoplasm with glycolysis, which splits one glucose molecule into two smaller molecules and yields a small amount of ATP without needing oxygen. The rest of the process happens inside the mitochondria, where the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain release far more energy. When oxygen is scarce, as in a hard-working muscle, cells fall back on fermentation, which produces much less ATP and leaves lactic acid behind. ATP acts like a rechargeable battery: the cell spends it to power movement, pumping and building molecules, and respiration recharges it.

## Chloroplasts and photosynthesis

Plant cells also contain chloroplasts, where photosynthesis converts light energy, water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen. The green pigment chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green light, which is why leaves look green. Photosynthesis happens in two linked stages. In the light-dependent reactions, light energy splits water molecules, releasing oxygen and storing energy in ATP and NADPH. In the Calvin cycle, the cell uses that stored energy to turn carbon dioxide from the air into sugar. Because the oxygen we breathe comes from split water molecules, photosynthesis is the source of almost all the oxygen in the atmosphere. Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are therefore linked: the products of one are the starting materials of the other.

## From DNA to protein

The nucleus stores the cell's genetic material in the form of DNA. A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for making one protein. During transcription, the gene's DNA sequence is copied into a molecule of messenger RNA inside the nucleus. The messenger RNA then leaves the nucleus and travels to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm. During translation, ribosomes read the RNA code three letters at a time and assemble amino acids into a chain that folds into a protein. Each three-letter group, called a codon, specifies one amino acid or tells the ribosome to stop. Because every protein is built this way, a change in a gene can change the protein it codes for, which is how mutations can alter how a cell works.

## Cell division

Cells reproduce by dividing. Before a cell divides, it copies all of its DNA so that each new cell receives a complete set of instructions. In mitosis, one cell divides into two genetically identical daughter cells, which is how the body grows and repairs damaged tissue. Meiosis is a different kind of division that produces sex cells with half the usual number of chromosomes, so that fertilisation restores the full number. Cell division is tightly controlled by checkpoints that stop the cycle if the DNA is damaged. When these controls fail, cells can divide without limit, which is what happens in cancer.
